blocks.text: that an oil is obtained from mastic, as from other kinds of resin (صمغ [ṣamgh] צמגים [ṣmgym]) (Ki tissa 76^{b}).
Tournefort (d. 1708. Tschirch 1, 906) reported on the production of mastic on the island of Chios (Scio).
Arabic مصطكى [maṣṭakā] is a loanword (Fraenkel 151); it has also migrated further into Armenian (Hübschmann 248. ZDMG. 51, 304) and into the European languages.

For Arabic: E. Wiedem. LVI 340. mastik (P.) Vullers 2, 51 = رَمَاسى [ramāsī]. מצטכי [mṣṭky] Abulw. 302 Bacher. Sha 1879, Syriac كيا [kyā] 1756. Physicians: Sha loc. cit. Kašef = كيا [kyā]. Abu Salt: משטיגי [mšṭygy]. Estori ha-Farḥī writes מצטכא [mṣṭkʾ] and, in the name of his father, identifies it with קטף [qṭp] (f 421^{b} Ven., 107^{b} Edelm., p. 662 Luncz).
Mastic is adulterated with the resin of the ʾubhul (juniper): Ibn Bassām in E. Wiedem. XL 177. 189.

Romance forms among Jews: משתיק [mštyq] (Abulw. 302 Bacher), מסתיקי [mstyqy], מסתיצי [mstyṣy] Mb. 31. 50. Menaḥem b. Salomo (1139) says: lōṭ is the resin of the tree שטינקי [šṭynqy] (lentisco). In Italian it is called: משטיכו [mšṭykw]; it is a remedy and serves to strengthen the teeth (Sechel tob p. XI.). — Grünbaum, Jüd.-span. Chrest. 11 f.: almastig, almaciga משטיק [mšṭyq] (Semag lāwīn 65 f. 22^{a}). On account of the blessings due for its fragrance, Tur and SchA OCh. 216, 3 mention it, in the codices as מצטכי [mṣṭky], in Zēdā lederech 64^{b} as מצתכין [mṣtkyn], מצטיכי [mṣṭyky], מסטיכי [msṭyky].

Since Luther had rendered צרי [ṣŏrī]*) in Ez. 27, 17 as mastic, this was frequently repeated and is still retained by Rothstein in the Kautzsch Bible (on ^{c d e}) and others. ṣŏrī is not mastic but storax (Flora 3, 390), as Rashi on ^{a}) quite correctly states. In accordance with our usage one translates "balm" (Rothstein), just as Abulwalīd renders it periphrastically as „tirjāḳ“, and as does the Geonic explanation in Ibn Ezra, which understands by it a remedy compounded of 75 ingredients — that is, a theriac.

When Targ. j substitutes שרף (ו)קטף [śrp (w)qṭp] for it, it will mean storax. In any case Onkelos with שעיף [šʿyp], Samaritan שעבה [šʿbh] (variant readings שעפה [šʿph], שעבי [šʿby], שאבה [šʾbh]), means not mastic but probably storax, not "balm" in general. The Syriac and Greek versions read in Sir. 6, 16 צרי חיים [ṣŏrī ḥayyîm], but the reading of the Hebrew text, צרור חיים [ṣərôr ḥayyîm], must be acknowledged as correct. — Susanna and Daniel 54—58 p. 138 Kautzsch does not belong here. — Boch. Hieroz. 1, 628 wanted to derive ῥητίνη [rhētinē] from ṣŏrī. Wrong is the combination of Roubinovitch, ḥiddūšīm 6, that Biblical Hebrew עזק [ʿzq] means the same as צרי [ṣŏrī].
